Rare earth element (REE) markets, where supply chains are highly concentrated across stages, particularly for refining, is a clear example. This paper quantifies the costs of de-risking supply chains using a dynamic global trade model calibrated with detailed market, industry and geological data. In the model, upstream (mining) and downstream (refining) production is slow-moving and determined by investment in capacity (CAPEX). To illustrate the model's properties, we evaluate how different policies can decrease downstream REE exposure from any single supplier by comparing CAPEX subsidies and stylized revenue-support policies under unilateral and simultaneous action among various importers. De-risking supply chains through targeted industrial policies is fiscally costly, although less so if pursued simultaneously by various importers. The fiscal cost of downstream unilateral CAPEX subsidies, for example, drops from 134% of the annual U.S. REE market (about 1.13 billion dollars) by 2035, to 90% under simultaneous action by other REE importers. Of course, de-escalation of trade tensions remains the first-best outcome.

paragraph_content.content: Interdependencies created by decades of globalization and the explosive growth of cross-border supply chains have become increasingly weaponized. Over the last decade, countries have progressively resorted to tariffs, sanctions, export controls, and other economic tools to pursue geopolitical objectives, most recently in the form of Western restrictions on semiconductors and Chinese restrictions on critical minerals (Dürr and Heilmann, 2025). As a result, global supply chains — long shaped exclusively by cost optimization — now face potential disruptions and geoeconomic fragmentation. For policymakers in import-dependent countries, this raises questions about how to de-risk critical supply chains and which industrial policies are best suited to do so.

These questions are important in global markets for rare earth elements (REEs), which saw the introduction of export licensing requirements and industrial policy announcements in 2025. A chokepoint is more likely to emerge when an input is difficult to substitute and three further conditions align: (i) extreme geographic concentration in a single country, (ii) a potential for disruption and, (iii) barriers to rapid diversification. Rare earths satisfy all three. On April 4, 2025, shortly after the U.S. imposed higher import tariffs on most of its trading partners, China — the world’s top producer of rare earth elements across all segments of the value chain including mining and refining — introduced export licensing requirements for seven REEs and permanent magnets, citing national security concerns and international non-proliferation obligations (Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, 2025). These export licensing requirements caused dramatic slowdowns in magnet exports to the rest of the world between April and June, but proved short-lived, with monthly Chinese export volumes quickly returning to their positive trend and displaying double-digit year-on-year growth rates.
In response, several countries have launched industrial policies aimed at de-risking REE production.

These supply chain disruptions and new industrial policies to build alternative supply chains all highlight the urgent need to better understand the economics of rare earths. To this end, this paper asks: how achievable are meaningful levels of REE supply chain de-risking under alternative industrial policy scenarios over the next decade, and at what fiscal cost? We find that while substantial relative to the size of the market, the fiscal costs associated with the required industrial policies would likely be manageable, particularly under simultaneous actions among various importing countries.

paragraph_content.content: To analyze alternative industrial policies, we develop a calibrated, dynamic trade model of the global rare earths market featuring two stages of production: mining (upstream) and refining (downstream). In the first stage, miners extract raw REE compounds and sell them to refiners on a global market for unprocessed REEs. Refiners then separate these compounds into REE oxides, which are sold on a global market to manufacturers such as permanent magnet producers. In each country/block, a representative miner and a representative refiner invest in productive capacity to maximize profits, taking prices as given.

The model is calibrated to the global market for rare earths by partitioning the world into six countries/regions: the US, China and Myanmar (which, following industry convention, is referred to as China+), Europe, Japan, other Anglophone countries (Canada, Australia), and rest-of-world (RoW). This partitioning reflects each country or region's role in the REE supply chain — as a major producer (China+), a significant consumer (Japan, Europe), a source of untapped mining potential (Anglophone countries), or an economy actively pursuing supply chain de-risking through industrial policy (the US) — with some countries spanning multiple roles.

The model calibration draws on detailed market, industry, and geological data, with particular attention to mining and refining costs across countries. We follow a two-step procedure. First, baseline cost parameters are derived from a breakeven analysis of rare earth projects worldwide. For producers outside China, we evaluate 21 feasibility studies, computing rare earth breakeven prices (in $/kg) after harmonizing key parameters such as discount rates. For China, breakeven costs are inferred from the 2006–2010 period, when China held a near-monopoly in REE production and the domestic industry was highly competitive, making observed prices a reasonable proxy for marginal costs.

Because cost data by production stage in China are not directly observed, the mining–refining decomposition is implemented transparently as a calibration assumption disciplined by project-level evidence from other producing countries and by the model's price and production targets. Second, taking the baseline cost parameters as given, slope parameters of the cost functions are calibrated to match each country's observed mining and refining production shares. Together, these two steps anchor the cost calibration in both forward-looking project-level estimates and historically revealed cost advantages.

paragraph_content.content: Next, we ask the model to quantify the impact of a major supply disruption, which we proxy by simulating a hypothetical fragmentation of global REE markets into two blocks. We use the model to assess the effects of two industrial policies designed to mitigate the potential macroeconomic effect of the supply disruption: investment subsidies and stylized downstream revenue-support policies (henceforth also referred to as price floors) applied to refining/oxide separation (the most crucial processing stage). We study two implementation scenarios: (1) unilateral action by the United States, in which the policy instruments apply only to U.S.-based producers, and (2) simultaneously among all various net importing countries (U.S., EU, Japan, Australia, and other economies), in which instruments are applied uniformly across participating countries.

To illustrate the trade offs involved with each policy, instruments are calibrated to increase the share of domestic rare earth consumption that is not dependent on the largest import source by 15 percentage points in the U.S., from 10 to 25 percent. This measure of diversification can be interpreted as a metric of exposure to the dominant supplier. This is 15 percentage points higher than our baseline at unchanged policies and in line with IEA projections that imply—under announced projects outside China and stated government policies—that diversification levels outside of China would increase by 16 percentage points, from 8 to 24 percent, over the next decade (International Energy Agency, 2025).

The quantitative results from the industrial policy simulations are as follows. First, sizable interventions are needed to attain the 25 percent de-risking targets. For example, in unilateral (simultaneous) scenarios the investment subsidy must cover 74.4 (74.0) percent of total investment costs to reach the 25 percent de-risking benchmark by 2035. This rises to 88.7 (87.9) percent to achieve 50 percent de-risking. As for revenue-support instrument (price floor), the required policy intervention is also sizable: 2.18x (2.0x) of the period market price for the unilateral (simultaneous) scenario. These large policy interventions reflect the relative efficiency of Chinese producers but also point to important price effects. Because there are already large capacities in both mining and refining, boosting production in a well-supplied market depresses prices and profits, which reduces private investment incentives and, all else equal, requires more generous government interventions to induce additional capacity.

paragraph_content.content: Second, investment subsidies are typically more fiscally efficient than the price floors when evaluated in present-value terms. This reflects the fact that investment subsidies are targeted at new capacity, whereas the revenue-support instrument also generates windfall gains for incumbent producers by supporting existing production. As a result, for a given de-risking target, the net present value of subsidy payments is lower than that of revenue support through price floors. To achieve the 25 percent target under the unilateral (simultaneous) scenario, U.S. fiscal costs associated with the investment subsidy over the first decade amount to 134 (90) percent of the U.S. REE market size—equivalent to about $1.13 billion ($0.76 billion).

At the same time, investment subsidies are more costly in the short term than price floors as they front-load fiscal outlays, with costs declining in the long term once investment is largely limited to replacing depreciated capital.

Third, simultaneous action among various importers reduces the fiscal cost of achieving a given de-risking target. For example, when the participating net-REE importing economies simultaneously incentivize investment in refining, individual countries' de-risking is achieved through a less concentrated buildup of capacity, as part of the fiscal cost is outsourced to participating countries. Under simultaneous action, those economies can also leverage the U.S. relatively higher efficiency in REEs processing and see substantial gains in de-risking, at comparatively lower fiscal costs.

Fourth, fiscal costs increase disproportionately with the degree of industrial policy intervention. For example, with higher CAPEX subsidies the U.S. can attain higher levels of de-risking levels in the downstream market, but the fiscal cost increases faster than the attained de-risking rate. This result suggests that very high levels of de-risking can be extremely costly, whereas moderate levels are quickly achievable and at moderate costs.

paragraph_content.content: Contribution to the literature. Our paper contributes to the literature on geoeconomics, which studies how countries leverage economic interdependencies to pursue geopolitical objectives (Clayton et al., 2026). Within this literature, Clayton et al. (2024) develop a theory of economic coercion in which large powers exploit trade and financial dependencies, highlighting the risks of highly concentrated supply chains. Kooi (2025) complements this perspective by formalizing the national security externality — the idea that markets may undervalue resilience in strategic sectors — and quantifies the value of reshoring semiconductor production capacity to the US. On the policy side, Baquie et al. (2025) argue that the effectiveness of industrial policies depends critically on careful design, with poorly targeted interventions yielding limited gains. While these contributions provide useful conceptual frameworks, the literature rarely quantifies the costs and effectiveness of specific policy instruments within particular supply chains, with Kooi (2025) being a notable exception for semiconductors.

We contribute by developing a calibrated dynamic model of the global rare earth supply chain that incorporates investment decisions in both mining and refining capacity and allows the evaluation of alternative policy instruments, including investment subsidies and price floors. The model captures the mining-to-refining bottleneck that characterizes rare earth supply chains, distinguishing between upstream extraction and the technologically more complex refining stage where global supply is most concentrated. Our results provide a cost-based rationale for the thesis in Clayton et al. (2024) that for chokepoint inputs, modest diversification can substantially improve resilience: we find that fiscal costs rise exponentially as de-risking targets increase, so that a small amount of supply chain diversification delivers the largest gains per dollar spent.

A second strand of the literature examines how trade restrictions reshape critical mineral supply chains. Chen (2025) examines mineral export restrictions as a form of industrial policy and finds that such policies reduce upstream exports while sometimes encouraging downstream processing, although empirical evidence of broader industrial upgrading remains limited. Kee and Xie (2025) study Indonesia's nickel export ban and show that while the policy succeeded in attracting foreign investment and raising the domestic value added ratio of exports, it also led to the entry of less efficient firms, highlighting the unintended allocative costs of such interventions. Turning to rare earths specifically, Alfaro et al. (2025) study how the 2010 REE supply shortage induced directed technological change in downstream industries abroad, increasing efficiency in the use of REEs and reshaping trade patterns in REE-intensive sectors. Shifting to the importer perspective, Shao et al. (2026) shows that a substantial share of global REE consumption occurs indirectly through manufactured goods exported by China, implying that dependence on Chinese REEs is significantly larger than raw mineral trade statistics suggest. Our paper contributes to this literature by developing a quantitative framework that jointly models upstream extraction and downstream processing across countries, allowing us to evaluate how specific industrial policy interventions such as subsidies and price floors reshape global REE production and trade patterns.

A third strand of the literature assesses the criticality of REEs and the macroeconomic consequences of supply disruptions. Nassar et al. (2015, 2020) develop frameworks for assessing mineral supply risk, identifying REEs as among the most strategically exposed inputs due to their concentrated production and importance for high-technology industries.

Relatedly, Bogmans et al. (2026) quantify how a REE supply shock propagates through input–output networks, amplifying GDP losses across advanced economies. Our paper builds on these findings by developing a dynamic model of the global REE supply chain that can assess how investment and production decisions respond to policy interventions over time. Rather than tracing the macroeconomic effects through input–output networks as in Bogmans et al. (2026), we study the impact of a market bifurcation on the REE supply chain itself, disentangling the effects on upstream and downstream markets.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 documents key features of REE markets and supply chains, including the greater geographical concentration in refining than in mining, that motivate the structure of the quantitative model. Section 3 presents a dynamic trade model of global markets for raw and refined REEs, and Section 4 describes the calibration strategy. Section 5 reports the quantitative results, including the effects of different industrial policies in various net-REE importing countries, and the trade-off between fiscal costs and de-risking targets. Section 6 concludes.

paragraph_content.content: This section highlights three key empirical features of REE markets that motivate the structure of the model. First, a small number of elements capture most of the market value. Second, geographical concentration is greater in processing than in mining. Third, this concentration has proved remarkably persistent across several price-spike episodes, particularly in processing.

title_content.content: 2.1 The Concentrated Economics of Rare Earths

paragraph_content.content: REEs are a group of 17 chemically similar metals, typically grouped into light (LREEs) and heavy (HREEs) based on atomic weight. HREEs are significantly less abundant in the earth's crust than LREEs and typically occur in lower concentrations, making them more difficult to extract at scale. Rare earths are employed in small quantities in various manufacturing sectors including automotive production, wind energy, military applications, semiconductors, and consumer electronics. They provide unique properties that are difficult to replicate cheaply, notably in applications requiring strong magnetic performance, thermal stability, or high-power density.

The economics of rare earths are highly concentrated. Four elements—neodymium (Nd) and praseodymium (Pr), both LREEs, and dysprosium (Dy) and terbium (Tb), both HREEs account for 96 percent of total rare earth oxide (REO) market value despite representing only 23 percent of production by weight (Morgan Stanley Research, 2025). Two forces drive this imbalance. On the demand side, permanent magnets—the fastest-growing application of rare earths—account for roughly 75–85 percent of total REE demand by value (International Energy Agency, 2025).

On the supply side, the natural composition of deposits skews production toward high-abundance, low-value elements such as lanthanum and cerium, while the "magnet-4" are produced in much smaller quantities. The economic weight of the magnet-4 has risen markedly since 2015, as investments in wind power and electric vehicles following the Paris Agreement have lifted demand for neodymium magnets.

title_content.content: 2.2 Global Supply Chain Structure and Concentration by Stage

paragraph_content.content: The rare earth supply chain consists of four sequential stages. Ore is first extracted and transported to nearby benefaction facilities, where mechanical and chemical processes concentrate it into a mixed rare earth compound. This intermediate product is then subjected to solvent extraction, a technically demanding process involving hundreds of sequential separation steps, to isolate individual rare earth elements into oxides or other compounds. In the final stage, these materials are reduced to their metallic form and combined with other inputs to produce alloys, such as NdFeB permanent magnets (U.S. Department of Energy, 2022).

During the 2000s China grew to become the primary source of global rare earth supply, reflecting technical expertise acquired over decades, a large domestic market, established infrastructure, extensive and farsighted policy support, and relatively flexible regulations. Today, China's primary position varies significantly by rare earth type and supply chain stage. Diversification has been most pronounced for the mining of LREEs: China's share of global LREE mining peaked at roughly 97 percent in 2010 and has since declined to around 58 percent in 2024 (Figure 1) (Nassar et al., 2023; U.S. Geological Survey, 2026). New production from Australia, the United States, and Myanmar has contributed to this shift.

page_footnote_content.content: Permanent magnets rely predominantly on Nd and Pr, which together account for approximately 85 percent of REE inputs in magnet production, with smaller but performance-critical contributions from Dy and, to a lesser extent, Tb (Alonso et al., 2023) (Appendix Table 1).

paragraph_content.content: Despite a trend of diversification in the mining of LREEs, China remains the leader over downstream processing stages, accounting for approximately 85–90 percent of global oxide separation capacity and 90–95 percent of metal refining (Figure 2) (Bedford, 2025). Separation is the central technical bottleneck in the supply chain. It is capital- and energy-intensive, environmentally damaging, and requires highly specialized expertise and intellectual property developed over decades. As a result, most rare earth concentrates, regardless of where they are mined, are shipped to China for processing. This limits the extent to which upstream diversification translates into overall supply chain diversification.

Furthermore, for HREEs, concentration is even more extreme and operates at every stage. As shown in Figure 2, which groups China (including Myanmar) accounts for 98 percent of mining, 96.5 percent of oxide separation, 95 percent of metal refining, and 89.5 percent of permanent magnet manufacturing.
Unlike LREEs, HREEs face a dual structural bottleneck: mining has seen virtually no geographic diversification, compounding the processing constraints documented above.

In short, for LREEs, the critical supply chain vulnerability lies not in mining—which has diversified — but in processing, where concentration remains entrenched. For HREEs, the challenge is more fundamental as both mining and processing currently exhibit a high degree of geographic concentration.

While China dominates permanent magnet manufacturing, this segment presents comparatively lower barriers to capacity expansion, with established producers already operating in the United States, Japan, and Europe — though at smaller scale than in China.

title_content.content: 2.3 Persistence of Concentration: Technology, Costs, and Lead Times

paragraph_content.content: Despite rising demand, some temporary supply shortages, and a wave of industrial policy interventions since 2025, diversification in REE supply chains has remained slow. This persistence reflects the interaction of technological complexity, high capital intensity, and unfavorable project economics outside established production hubs. The concentration in separation and refining in China reflects decades of accumulated technical knowledge and infrastructure that are not easily replicated, while the regulatory burden and specialized expertise required for processing make entry difficult even under favorable market conditions.

New REE projects outside China also face long lead times, typically requiring 10–15 years or more to move from discovery to commercial production, owing to permitting, environmental regulation, financing, and process development (International Energy Agency, 2025). New entrants must replicate not only physical infrastructure but also the tacit knowledge embedded in production processes, further raising effective entry costs.

Project-level economics reinforce these constraints. A bottom-up assessment of 21 REE projects outside China reveals substantial dispersion in capital and operating costs, with many projects situated on the upper end of the global cost curve (Figure 13). Only a limited number of projects are profitable at current price levels, while many require substantially higher prices to become viable. Historical price dynamics have compounded this problem: following the 2010–2011 price spike, REE prices declined sharply and remained subdued for an extended period, and broader price volatility has since made it difficult to justify the large and irreversible investments required to develop new capacity outside China.

China's introduction of REE export licensing requirements in April 2025 triggered an immediate market slowdown: permanent magnet exports fell by roughly 70 percent year-on-year at the trough, while Dy and Tb prices in European markets nearly tripled by mid-2025. Although monthly Chinese export volumes quickly returned to trend growth—displaying double-digit year-on-year growth rates—the episode was followed by accelerated industrial policy efforts across major economies aimed at de-risking supply chains. It remains to be seen whether these efforts will materially alter existing dependencies.

These efforts have focused on three approaches. First, price floors and offtake agreements have been concluded to provide investment certainty in volatile markets, as many REE projects are not commercially viable at current neodymium prices (about $55/kg). A July 2025 agreement between the U.S. government and MP Materials introduced a price-protection mechanism for key REE products, and price floors more broadly featured prominently in high-level G7 critical minerals discussions. In the quantitative analysis below, we capture this policy family with a stylized revenue-support instrument for refiners; this should be interpreted as a tractable proxy for downside protection rather than as a literal state-contingent contract. Second, governments have provided direct financial support—through equity stakes, loans, and grants—to supply capital and signal long-term commitment. Third, international agreements signed in October 2025 between the United States and Japan, Malaysia, Thailand, and Australia, alongside the G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan, promote joint financing and coordinated procurement, mobilizing an estimated $6.4 billion in public and private funding to de-risk REE supply chains.

page_footnote_content.content: While the barriers to diversification documented above are formidable, geological scarcity per se is not among them, at least for LREEs. Global REE reserves outside China exceed 41 million tons of rare earth oxide equivalent, distributed across Brazil, Australia, Russia, Vietnam, United States, and several other jurisdictions (U.S. Geological Survey, 2026), and mine production of LREEs outside of China and Myanmar already reached 98,000 tons in 2025, accounting for 25 percent of global output (U.S. Geological Survey, 2026). For heavy rare earths the picture is fundamentally different: nearly all commercially viable HREE deposits are concentrated in southern China and Myanmar (Bedford, 2025), and current production and proven reserves in other jurisdictions are insufficient to support comparable self-sufficiency targets. That said, proven reserves are not exogenous—Arezki et al. (2019) show that an increase in a country’s market orientation leads to a significant increase in mineral discoveries, suggesting that current reserve estimates understate the resource base that would emerge under sustained exploration incentives outside China. HREE supply chain diversification is thus hampered by both geological scarcity and processing concentration, a dimension the current model does not explicitly capture but which constitutes an important avenue for future research.

This section analyzes the quantitative implications of the global REE model described in this paper. First, we begin by presenting the results arising from simulating the model under current policies. We further expand the discussion of the structure of the global REE market by examining the supply and demand elasticities. Second, we describe the consequences of a potential global REE supply shock. Third, we discuss the effects of introducing different industrial policies in net importing economies, focusing our attention on the special case of the US.

Fourth, we show that the fiscal cost of industrial policies is convex in the degree of attained de-risking. Throughout this section we refer to "importing countries" and "economies outside China" interchangeably as in the special case of REEs, and given the current market structure, the two groups coincide.
Using the calibration strategy outlined above, we simulate the model for a period of T = 150 years starting in 2025.

In the model we use as initial conditions the observed levels of mining and refining quantities in 2024, outlined in Table 1. We feed the model with the anticipated demand growth rates described in Table 1 and construct the paths of mining and refining output, final good demand, and price levels. We report the results of the baseline in Figure 4.

The projected increase in demand raises mining and refining production across all the economies, with only modest changes in their distributions across countries. In the case of the U.S., the increase in refined REE production leads to only a marginal improvement in de-risking relative to China. The price of the refined REE good increases on impact to accommodate the initial excess demand from consumers, and rises further during the period of stronger demand between 2030 and 2034. As demand growth stabilizes and investment in mining and refining increases, prices begin to decline and converge to a new steady state. In the new steady state, equilibrium prices remain higher, due to the quadratic functional forms of OPEX and CAPEX.

paragraph_content.content: The increase in demand stimulates further mined and refined output through higher CAPEX investment in both stages. In particular, investment in refining capacity is stronger. Interestingly, demand growth leads to faster growth in economies outside China. Intuitively, by considering (11) and (12), and noting that marginal OPEX and CAPEX are linear, demand growth leads to higher net mining and refining profit margins. Prior to demand growth, producers outside China, and in particular refiners, faced thinner margins compared to their Chinese competitors. Hence, the improvement in profit margins is relatively larger for these economies, allowing them to capture a greater share of the increased demand for the final product. This is confirmed by the observation that investment grows faster outside China and that the new steady state rate of investment is higher. The top right panel in Figure 4 shows that Chinese market leadership in mining and refining is reduced, although by a small margin. Moreover, demand growth leads to persistently higher price levels for both upstream and downstream products, with initially higher prices driven by strong investment needs and supply rigidities.

The short-run elasticities of demand and supply are close to zero, indicating a limited ability to adjust quantities for both miners and refiners in the short run. Overall, these findings highlight a pronounced distinction between short-run and long-run dynamics in the REE market.

paragraph_content.content: Table 4 describes the first-pass consequences of the shock. On the one hand, in the market for mined products, the impact would generate a positive excess supply, as China is a net importer of mined inputs for refining. This would result in a 10.78% increase in net supply in markets outside China. On the other hand, the impact of the market fragmentation on the refining market would be substantial. As China accounts for around 92% of the global supply of refined products, the shock to pre-shock net importers would be large. At the same time, since China also demands around 50% of refined products, net-REE importers would experience a net supply shock of approximately -42%.

We evaluate the effects of this shock on net-REE importing countries. We consider a scenario in which these economies start from their respective 2024 demand and supply levels and, unexpectedly, the market becomes segmented at time t = 2025. As noted above, since the relative production of mined and refined products across these economies outside China is determined by the slope of the marginal CAPEX costs, the impact of the shock is symmetric across all countries. We report the results of this supply disruption scenario in Figure 5.

paragraph_content.content: On impact, the supply disruption causes a sharp increase in prices in both markets, i.e., the market for mined and refined products. In the first year, the price of refined REEs spikes to almost 80 times the baseline price, while mined REE products experience a smaller increase, around 7.4 times the baseline price. The structure of the downstream market plays a key role. Since refineries outside China are less productive than Chinese ones, the shock has a much larger impact on refining than on mining. Additionally, the price of mined products is partially capped by the positive net supply shock in the upstream market, as China is a net importer of raw materials.

The increase in prices plays two roles. First, it reduces demand for refined REE products, which falls by around 48% on impact. Second, it stimulates investment in refining capacity, leading to a more than threefold increase in the supply of refined products. The expansion in refining, in turn, raises demand for mined inputs, which increases to about 1.3 times its baseline level. As a result, the equilibrium price of mined products also rises on impact, although less than that of refined products. Despite the initial positive net supply shock for miners outside of China, the disruption in the downstream market is large enough to drive up both prices and increase upstream production in order to restore equilibrium in the downstream market. The strong response of prices, combined with the limited adjustment of quantities, highlights the low supply and demand elasticities of the REE market in the short run.

In the long run, CAPEX investment in both upstream and downstream markets gradually expands capacity. As a result, mining (refining) output rises to about 2.1 (4.5) times its pre-shock level, and prices begin to decline relatively quickly. In the upstream market, the equilibrium price falls from 7.4 to 1.7 times the baseline price, remaining about 70% above the baseline. Similarly, in the downstream market, the equilibrium price of refined products declines from 80 to 2.5 times the baseline, i.e., about 150% above baseline. The combination of higher production and lower prices allows final consumers to recover part of the lost demand relatively quickly, which converges to around 89% of its baseline level, implying a long run loss of about 11% of the baseline demand. Contrary to the short run, quantities adjust more flexibly in the long run, highlighting our finding that supply and demand elasticities of the REE market are higher in the long run.

In response to rising vulnerabilities in REE supply, countries and firms are adopting a range of adaptation strategies. Stockpiling provides a short-term buffer against disruptions, but does not address underlying structural dependence, while recycling offers longer-term potential, although it cannot yet serve as a primary supply source. Reshoring and import diversification have emerged as the main medium-term responses, despite uncertain viability given long development timelines, coordination challenges, and potential shortages of skilled labor.

Because reshoring is costly, policymakers must balance efficiency losses in normal times against expected disruption losses in crisis periods. Optimal de-risking is best understood as an insurance policy: the premium paid in normal times (efficiency losses) should be commensurate with the expected damage in crisis times (disruption losses). Moreover, security benefits are likely to exhibit diminishing returns, with the first 10-20 percent increase in de-risking delivering the largest reduction in vulnerability. This means that even modest increases in de-risking can substantially reduce vulnerability to supply disruptions at relatively low efficiency costs (Clayton et al., 2024).

To improve the degree of de-risking, which we define as the total consumption of refined REEs that is either produced at home or from other countries other than the market leader, we ask the model to assess the effects of two industrial policies (investment subsidies and stylized revenue-support policies) applied to refiners, under two implementation scenarios: (1) unilateral action by the United States, in which the policy instruments apply only to U.S.-based producers, and (2) simultaneous action among all importing countries (U.S., EU, Japan, Australia, and other economies), in which instruments are applied uniformly across participating countries. Because trade in the model is frictionless and homogeneous, the resulting country-level de-risking statistics should be interpreted as reduced-form concentration measures rather than literal bilateral sourcing predictions. We focus on refiners only because, as discussed above, a global supply shock primarily affects the downstream segment, while the impact on miners is more limited.

We start by selecting a constant CAPEX subsidy rate (or revenue-support rate) that would allow the U.S., in this example, to reach a 25% level of de-risking by 2035. This is 15 percentage points higher than our baseline and in line with IEA projections which show that, under currently announced projects outside China and stated government policies, de-risking levels outside of China would rise from about 8 percent to roughly 24 percent over the next decade. We then compare the fiscal cost of achieving the same benchmark increase in de-risking for the U.S. by allowing all importer countries to simultaneously implement similar policies. The same kind of exercise with very similar results could have been run focusing on either one of the importing countries of our model. We then repeat the same exercise for a more ambitious target of 50%.

(i) For a given policy instrument, simultaneous action reduces the fiscal cost to achieve a given level of de-risking fo the U.S. and all participating countries. As all net REEs importers increase their output, the U.S. can attain higher de-risking levels with a smaller expansion in domestic production and relying more on imports from other participating countries, thereby limiting fiscal costs even when policy rates are comparable (or slightly higher). In a similar fashion, as simultaneous action increases global REE output more than unilateral action, part of the increment is absorbed by consumption in all other countries, who successfully manage to partially de-risk their supply chain.

(ii) The fiscal cost of CAPEX subsidies is initially higher than that of the revenue-support policy, but substantially lower in the long run. On the one hand, investment precedes production during growth phases. Therefore, CAPEX subsidies frontload fiscal costs in the early years, with lower costs later on as investment needs decline. On the other hand, the price floor backloads fiscal costs: as production and prices rise over time, fiscal costs increase and remain elevated as the economy converges towards a new steady state.

(iii) The fiscal cost increases faster than the increase in achieved de-risking levels. Taking unilateral revenue support as a reference, the cost of achieving 25% de-risking levels by 2035 is about 13.4% of baseline consumption in 2025, whereas the cost exceeds 44.5% if the U.S. was targeting 50% by 2035. In the long-run, the fiscal cost of the unilateral revenue-support policy stabilizes around 41.6% of baseline consumption for a 25% target, but rises to over 269% for the 50% target. Hence, doubling the de-risking target more than doubles the fiscal cost. Similar results are observed also for the other policy instruments.

Overall, for a 25% de-risking target, the total fiscal cost of industrial policies over the period 2025–2035 is large in terms of market size. CAPEX subsidies amount to 134% of the annual U.S. REE market under unilateral action and 90% under simultaneous action among various importers. The stylized revenue-support policies are significantly more expensive, reaching 248% under unilateral policies and 172% under simultaneous policies. paragraph_content.content: The Impact of Industrial Policies on the Global REE Market - While in our example these industrial policies improve U.S. de-risking levels, we also examine their spillover effects on other net-REE importing countries. As described above, under simultaneous action all of these participating economies adopt the same policy instrument and rate. Because the strategy of net-REE importers emphasizes de-risking, we focus on aggregate net-REE importers outcomes, rather than the outcome of the single country alone. Figure 8 reports the impact of CAPEX subsidies to refiners on China and other economies. The left-hand column shows results for policies targeting a 25% U.S. de-risking level by 2035, while the right-hand column reports results for the 50% target. We examine effects on mining and refining output, consumption of refined products, and prices:

(a) Mining - Under a 25% target, unilateral subsidies moderately increase mining output in both China and other economies, with a slightly larger effect outside China (+0.3%) than in China (+0.26%). Under a 50% target, unilateral subsidies increase Chinese mining output by 0.66%, while output in net importing countries increases by 0.79%. Under simultaneous action, both blocks experience larger increases in mining output due to stronger demand from refiners. Chinese mining output increases by 1.44% (2.8%) in the long-run for the 25% (50%) target, while output net importing countries increases by 1.72% (3.3%). Overall, industrial policies targeting refiners generate positive spillovers on miners in all countries.

(b) Refining - In contrast to mining, policies targeting refiners have diverging effects across regions. In China, refining output declines by 2.5% under unilateral subsidies and by 14.8% under simultaneous action for a 25% target. The effect is stronger under a 50% target, with declines of 6.8% and 27.7%, respectively. By contrast, refining output outside China increases substantially: by 25.9% (70.8%) under unilateral action and by 154.7% (290%) under simultaneous policies for the 25% (50%) de-risking target.

(c) Consumption - Industrial policies have relatively small effects on consumption. All countries are symmetrically affected by the policies, and global consumption increases by 0.27% under unilateral action with a 25% target, and by 1.5% under simultaneous policies. For a 50% de-risking target global consumption increases by 0.69% (2.91%) under unilateral (simultaneous) action.

(d) Prices - Price dynamics reflect the changes in mining and refining. Under unilateral subsidies, mining prices initially rise by 1.48% (3.82%) and settle at +0.17% (+0.49%) in the long-run for the 25% (50%) target. Under simultaneous subsidies, mining prices rise by 8.66% (17.66%) on impact and converge to +1.13% (+2.22%) in the long-run for the 25% (50%) target. In contrast, refining prices decline.

Under unilateral U.S. policies, U.S. de-risking increases, while that of other net importers remains broadly unchanged or even slightly declines. In contrast, simultaneous policies among importers allow both the U.S. and the other importing countries to increase their degree of de-risking. As shown in Figure 9, both simultaneous CAPEX subsidies and revenue-support policies improve the degree of de-risking for Japan and the EU. Since both start from relatively lower levels than the U.S., 6% and 8.9%, respectively, simultaneous actions allow them to achieve substantially higher independence relative to their baseline. While the U.S. attains 25% de-risking levels by 2035, the EU reaches 17.1% and Japan 23.1%. Relative to the simultaneous benchmark, unilateral U.S. policies leave the EU and Japan less de-risked because negative price spillovers crowd out part of the production response elsewhere; relative to their own baselines, however, the declines remain modest. Analogous results are observed for the simulation with a higher benchmark of 50% de-risking in the U.S..

Industrial policies also generate notable differences in fiscal costs across countries. Figure 10 reports the fiscal costs of simultaneous policies for the U.S., EU, and Japan. Simultaneous action allows the U.S. to shift part of the fiscal burden onto other net-REE importing countries. Focusing on the 25% target, the cost of CAPEX subsidies is nearly as high in Japan as in the U.S., while it is significantly lower in Europe. This reflects differences in refining activity: fiscal costs are higher in countries with larger refining sectors (such as the U.S. and Japan) and lower where refining activity is more limited. This pattern holds for both policy instruments and for the 50% de-risking target.

paragraph_content.content: This paper shows that disruptions to REE supplies could substantially affect supply chains. Avoiding trade tensions and restrictions remains the first-best outcome to promote steady REE supply. Model-based analysis suggests that de-risking supply chains through targeted industrial policies is fiscally costly. However, costs are lower if de-risking is pursued by various importers simultaneously and if policy instruments directly target the expansion of new production capacity. Focusing on CAPEX subsidies and price floor mechanisms, we found that simultaneous action allows participating countries to achieve higher levels of de-risking at relatively moderate fiscal costs, particularly when CAPEX subsidies are implemented. Future research could take a more granular view of the rare earth element complex, which, after all, consists of 17 distinct yet chemically related elements, with the aim of developing a framework that distinguishes between heavy (HREE) and light (LREE) elements and embeds these distinctions in the modeling of supply constraints. Additional policies – like stockpiling or re-shoring – could also be analyzed and the group of producer countries could be enlarged beyond China.

title_content.content: A Model calibration and incentive price methodology

paragraph_content.content: This section documents the data construction and project-level methodology used to calibrate the cost intercept parameters described in Section 4.3. The analysis is based on a bottom-up reconstruction of production, cost, and revenue characteristics for individual rare earth mining (plus processing) projects outside China. These project-level estimates are used to derive the incentive prices employed in Section 4.3 and to construct the economic supply curve shown in Figure 13.

Project scope and coverage. The dataset is constructed from a mine-by-mine assessment of rare earth projects located in Australia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, Canada, Greenland, Sweden, and the United States. Projects are included only where sufficient public documentation is available, such as technical reports, economic assessments, and prefeasibility or feasibility studies. These documents were identified primarily through the S&P Capital IQ Pro database and supporting project disclosures, occasionally supplemented with more recent publicly available information. The resulting dataset covers 21 non-Chinese projects with sufficient cost, production, and technical information to reconstruct project-level economic metrics.

Manual reconstruction of production profiles. For each project, technical documentation was manually reviewed to extract total rare earth oxide (TREO) production volumes, reported oxide distributions, and annual production quantities for individual rare earth oxides. These data were then used to identify the elements and corresponding annual production volumes that are economically relevant for the incentive price calculations.

Treatment of non-REE revenues. Where applicable, project documentation reports additional by-product revenues from non-rare earth elements. When detailed production data were available, annual volumes of these non-REE minerals were multiplied by corresponding commodity prices to estimate associated revenue streams. In some cases, projects report only nominal annual revenue figures for non-REE minerals, which were incorporated directly into the revenue calculations. However, the incentive price used to construct the supply curve in Figure 13 excludes non-REE revenues so that the break-even condition is determined solely by rare earth project economics.
Capital expenditure. Initial capital expenditures (CAPEX) were taken directly from project documentation. Where reported, sustaining capital expenditures were also included.

Operating expenditure. Operating costs (OPEX) were reconstructed from project documentation using one of three approaches depending on data availability. First, where total life-of-mine operating costs were reported, average annual OPEX was calculated as total life-of-mine operating costs divided by the expected mine lifespan. Second, where studies directly reported an average annual operating expense, this value was used as stated. Third, where operating costs were reported as a unit cost (US$ per kilogram of TREO), annual OPEX was calculated by multiplying the reported unit cost by average annual TREO production.

Inflation adjustment and discounting. All monetary values were converted to a common 2024–25 cost basis using a constant annual inflation rate of 2%. In addition, a uniform real discount rate of 8% was applied across all projects. These adjustments were applied consistently to CAPEX, OPEX, and revenue components in order to ensure comparability across projects with feasibility studies produced in different years.

Project classification and realized price factors. Projects were grouped into two categories: those producing mixed rare earth chemical products and those producing separated rare earth oxides. Projects producing mixed rare earth chemical products were assigned a realized price factor of 62.5%, while projects producing separated rare earth oxides were assigned a factor of 90%. These factors capture the difference in realized value between partially processed intermediate products and more refined separated oxides, and ensure that differences in processing depth are reflected consistently in project revenues.

Incentive price definition and break-even condition. For each project, we compute an NdPr-equivalent production metric by converting reported rare earth element revenues into an equivalent quantity expressed in NdPr terms. Specifically, we use all revenue information available in project economic documents (e.g., feasibility studies, economic analyses). For some projects, this consists only of revenues from neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, while for others it covers a broader set of rare earth elements (e.g., Lanthanum, Cerium, Gadolinium, Yttrium, Samarium, Europium). We aggregate these revenues and divide by the 2024 average NdPr oxide price, yielding an implied NdPr-equivalent production capacity:

This normalization converts a project's multi-element revenue stream into a single NdPr-equivalent production metric, effectively capturing the contribution of all reported rare earth elements into a common NdPr-based quantity.

page_footnote_content.content: Implicitly, the framework assumes that relative price ratios across elements remain fixed at their 2024 benchmark levels, so that a change in the NdPr price is representative of a proportional change across the rare earth price complex. While co-movement across elements is imperfect in practice, this assumption provides a tractable single-price metric for comparing projects across a heterogeneous deposit base.

paragraph_content.content: Construction of the economic supply curve. Using the project-level incentive prices defined in equation (23), projects are ranked in ascending order of break-even cost and aggregated cumulatively according to their production capacity. The horizontal axis of Figure 13 reports cumulative NdPr-equivalent production capacity in tons per annum, constructed by converting total project revenues into an equivalent quantity expressed in NdPr terms, while the vertical axis reports the corresponding incentive price in US$/kg of NdPr oxide. Both quantities and prices are therefore expressed in NdPr terms.

This procedure produces a stepwise economic supply curve that preserves project-level resolution while illustrating the cost distribution of potential non-Chinese rare earth supply.
